253.title: Christianity: the two commandments
253.hook: Jesus names the greatest commandments: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37–40)
253.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize the two great commandments, and some churches read them aloud in worship; churches of many traditions teach love of God and neighbor as the heart of the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pesach, the freedom meal. Your line was we were slaves, now free. Today, a new visit: Christianity.

Of all the commandments, which one is the greatest? There's no safe answer, and in the Gospel of Matthew a lawyer puts it to Jesus. The text says he asked it to test him. Jewish tradition, written down later, counts six hundred and thirteen commandments in the Torah. Pick one, and you seem to shrug at the rest. Jesus doesn't pick one. He picks two, and he picks them from the very scripture of last week's visit.
screen: `A QUESTION TO TEST HIM.` → `WHICH ONE IS THE GREATEST?` → `HE PICKS TWO.`

segments.voice: His answer, in the King James Version, Matthew twenty-two: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." If the first sounds familiar, it should. It comes from Deuteronomy, right beside the Shema from a week ago: hear, O Israel. The second comes from Leviticus, chapter nineteen. Jesus, a Jewish teacher, is quoting the Torah, and many Christians treat his pairing as the center of their faith. Notice three things. First, the order: God first, neighbor second, but the second is like unto it, the same kind of thing. Many Christians say you can't really keep one without the other; a later New Testament letter says that someone who claims to love God and hates a brother is not telling the truth. Second, the word hang: everything else hangs on these two, like a door on its hinges. Third, as thyself. It assumes you already know how you want to be treated, and asks you to aim that at someone else. In Luke's Gospel, a lawyer asks the follow-up, and who is my neighbor? Jesus answers with a story, the good Samaritan, in which the neighbor turns out to be the stranger no one expected.
screen: `LOVE GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART.` · `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.` · `ALL THE LAW HANGS ON THESE TWO.` · `WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR?` · then, large: `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR.`

segments.voice: Let faces come: the person next door, the coworker who seems tired, the stranger who serves your coffee. Pick one, and ask the as-yourself question: if I were them today, what small thing would I be glad of? A hand with the bins, a real hello, a message; let the answer be small and doable.
Christianity, at its center: two commandments, love God and love your neighbor as yourself, on which all the law and the prophets hang. Today's word.
Your line: love your neighbor. How you want to be treated is the measure. See you tomorrow.

254.title: Christianity: blessed are
254.hook: blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers (Matthew 5:3–9)
254.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize the Beatitudes, and churches read them often, especially on All Saints' Day; some use them as a daily examination of how they are living.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two commandments, love God and love your neighbor as yourself. Your line was love your neighbor.

Scroll through any feed for a minute and you'll see who the world calls blessed. The rich. The winners. The ones on the beach with the perfect caption. Hashtag blessed. Now a hillside in Galilee. Crowds have followed Jesus, and he goes up the mountain. He sits down, the way teachers did, and the first word out of his mouth is blessed. Then he names who's blessed, and it's almost the opposite list: the Beatitudes, the opening of the Sermon on the Mount.
screen: `HASHTAG BLESSED.` → `A HILLSIDE IN GALILEE.` → `ALMOST THE OPPOSITE LIST.`

segments.voice: Matthew chapter five, in the King James words: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Then those who mourn, who will be comforted. "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth." Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy." The pure in heart, who shall see God. And today's line: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." The Greek word behind blessed is makarios. It can mean happy, fortunate, well off, the word for someone whose life has turned out right. So the truly well off, Jesus says, are the grieving, the gentle, the merciful, the ones making peace. Each line has two halves: who, and what's coming to them. Many Christians read the second halves as promises about God's kingdom, partly now and fully later. Luke's Gospel has a shorter version, set on a level place, that says simply blessed be ye poor, and adds a set of woes. Christian readers set Matthew's poor in spirit beside Luke's plain poor, and they differ on how much to stress each. And notice the word in today's line: not peace-lovers, peacemakers. Making is work. It's the person who steps into the argument at the family dinner, or sends the first message after the fight.

Your line: blessed are the peacemakers. They'll be called children of God. Day two hundred fifty-four.

255.title: Christianity: the Lord's Prayer
255.hook: the prayer Jesus taught his followers (Matthew 6:9–13)
255.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians all pray the Lord's Prayer, many daily, and congregations often say it together; Catholics call it the Our Father and pray it in the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Beatitudes, and makarios, truly well off. Your line was blessed are the peacemakers.

Our Father, who art in heaven. Those six words travel a long way from any church: into school halls, hospital rooms, gravesides and old films. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants all pray what follows, each in their own language and their own version, with small differences in the wording. It all began with a simple request. In Luke's Gospel, the disciples watch Jesus pray and ask him: teach us.
screen: `OUR FATHER, WHO ART IN HEAVEN.` → `CATHOLIC, ORTHODOX, PROTESTANT.` → `TEACH US.`

segments.voice: Matthew chapter six, in the King James Version: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread." Then forgiveness, as we forgive others; then protection from temptation and evil. It's short on purpose: just before it, Jesus warns against heaping up words, as if length impressed God. Look at the shape. The first half faces God: the name, the kingdom, the will. The second half faces us: bread, forgiveness, protection. Big things, then small things, allowed in the same breath. Now today's line. The Greek word translated daily, epiousios, appears almost nowhere else in all of Greek writing, and nobody is certain what it means. Daily? For tomorrow? Needed for existence? Early Christian writers already argued about it, and some read it as the bread of the Eucharist too. However it's translated, the request is small: enough for today, not a year's supply. It echoes the manna in the wilderness, from the story of the going out from Egypt: bread that came each morning, enough for that day, and spoiled if hoarded. The endings differ. Many Protestants close with for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory. Luke's version doesn't have that line, and at Catholic Mass it comes a little later, after another short prayer.
screen: `TEACH US TO PRAY.` · `GOD'S NAME FIRST, THEN OUR BREAD.` · `EPIOUSIOS — NOBODY IS SURE.` · `ENOUGH FOR TODAY, LIKE MANNA.` · then, large: `DAILY BREAD.`

segments.voice: Read it slowly once, pausing at each line; if you pray, you can pray it, and if not, simply listen to the old words: Our Father which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, give us this day our daily bread. Then sit with that one line: what is enough, just for today?
Christianity, through the Lord's Prayer: the prayer Jesus taught, God's name first, then bread for today. Today's word.
Your line: daily bread. Enough for today; tomorrow's worries can wait. That's two hundred fifty-five.

256.title: Christianity: grace
256.hook: Christians speak of grace, God's love given before anything is earned
256.howItsDone: Many Christians say grace before meals, and churches speak of grace in preaching, baptism and communion; Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox Christians each describe how grace works in their own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Lord's Prayer, and a Greek word nobody can pin down. Your line was daily bread, enough for today.

Someone pays for your coffee. The person behind you in line, a stranger, and by the time you turn around they're gone. What's your first feeling? For a lot of people it isn't simple joy. It's a small itch. I should pay them back. I should pay it forward. I owe someone now. Keeping score comes easily; receiving something unearned doesn't. That itch is exactly where a central Christian word lands: grace.
screen: `A STRANGER PAYS FOR YOUR COFFEE.` → `THE ITCH: I OWE SOMEONE.` → `GRACE.`

segments.voice: The New Testament word is charis. In ordinary Greek it meant a favor, a gift, a kindness freely done, and the gratitude that answers it. Charisma grows from the same family; so does eucharist, thanksgiving, which is coming up next week. Paul's letters return to charis again and again. Here's Ephesians, in the King James Version: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." The gift comes first. Another letter, 1 John, puts it more briefly: "We love him, because he first loved us." Christians say God doesn't wait for people to become good enough to be loved. The love comes first, and goodness grows in answer to it. Where Christians differ is how grace and human response fit together. Martin Luther and the Protestant reformers stressed that people are made right with God by grace through faith alone, not by works. Catholic and Orthodox Christians also say grace comes first and can't be earned, and they speak of it working through the sacraments and through a person's free cooperation, growing over a lifetime. Those differences have been argued, sometimes bitterly, since the Reformation, and in 1999 Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint statement saying they now share a basic understanding. The hymn Amazing Grace was written by John Newton, who had once captained slave ships. In it he calls himself a wretch who was saved: a man singing about a gift he knew he hadn't earned.
screen: `CHARIS — A GIFT FREELY GIVEN.` · `NOT OF YOURSELVES: THE GIFT OF GOD.` · `HE FIRST LOVED US.` · `HOW GRACE AND RESPONSE FIT TOGETHER.` · then, large: `GIVEN, NOT EARNED.`

segments.voice: Remember a gift you were given that you didn't earn: a friend who stayed, a teacher who saw something in you, a second chance. Notice the urge to explain it away, or to pay it back right now, and let that urge go quiet. Just receive it, and let it land.
Grace. Charis in Greek: a gift freely given; for Christians, God's love that comes before anything is earned. Today's word.
Your line: given, not earned. The answer is thanks, not a ledger. See you tomorrow.

257.title: Christianity: Easter
257.hook: Christians believe Jesus died on the cross and rose again, and their hope rests there
257.howItsDone: Christians keep Holy Week before Easter, remembering the Last Supper and the crucifixion on Good Friday, then celebrate the resurrection on Easter Sunday, often with a vigil or sunrise service.

segments.voice: Yesterday: grace, charis, love that comes first. Your line was given, not earned.

Very early on a Sunday morning, before the sun is properly up, a few women walk to a graveyard carrying spices. They're going to do the last thing you can do for someone you loved: care for the body. The whole way, they've worried about something practical. The tomb was sealed with a heavy stone. Who's going to move it? When they arrive, the stone is already rolled away. Everything Christians hope for grows out of what they found, and didn't find, that morning.
screen: `EARLY SUNDAY, CARRYING SPICES.` → `WHO WILL MOVE THE STONE?` → `ALREADY ROLLED AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the Friday. Jesus was arrested in Jerusalem during Passover and crucified by the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for rebels and slaves, slow and public, meant to shame. His followers scattered. Then the Sunday. All four Gospels tell of the empty tomb, each a little differently: who went, how many angels, who they met. In Matthew, the angel tells the women, in the King James words: "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said." In John's Gospel, Mary Magdalene stays weeping by the tomb, thinks the man beside her is the gardener, and knows him only when he says her name. The earliest written account is older than the Gospels: a letter from Paul, written about twenty years after, passing on what he'd received, that Christ died, was buried, "and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures." Christians say this is the center of everything; Paul writes that if Christ has not been raised, their faith is in vain. Easter is the oldest and greatest Christian feast. In many languages it's called Pascha, from Pesach, because it happened at Passover. On Easter morning many Orthodox Christians greet each other, Christ is risen, and answer, he is risen indeed. Western and Orthodox churches often celebrate on different Sundays, because they calculate the date with different calendars. For Christians, the hope is not that death was avoided, but that it was gone through, and came out the other side as new life.
screen: `CRUCIFIED UNDER PONTIUS PILATE.` · `HE IS NOT HERE: HE IS RISEN.` · `MARY, AND HER NAME SPOKEN.` · `PASCHA, FROM PESACH.` · then, large: `NEW LIFE.`

segments.voice: Whatever you believe about that morning, hold the picture: a heavy stone, already moved. Bring to mind one thing in your life that feels sealed shut, a habit, a grief, a relationship. Don't force it open; just hold the question: what would new life look like here?
Christianity, through Easter: Jesus crucified and, Christians say, risen on the third day. Their hope rests there. Today's word.
Your line: new life. The stone was moved before anyone got there. Day two hundred fifty-seven, done.

258.title: Christianity: love is patient
258.hook: Paul's hymn to love: patient, kind, not envious (1 Corinthians 13, where the KJV says "charity")
258.howItsDone: 1 Corinthians 13 is read at many Christian weddings and funerals, and some Christians use its list, patient, kind, not envious, as a daily check on how they treat others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Easter, the stone already rolled away. Your line was new life.

If you've been to a wedding, you've probably heard it. Someone's cousin walks to the front, unfolds a piece of paper, and reads: love is patient, love is kind. Everyone nods. It's lovely. It fits on a card. But the man who wrote it wasn't thinking about weddings at all. He was writing to a church that was falling apart: people suing each other, showing off, forming cliques, looking down on the ones with less. Today: Paul's chapter on love, and the fight it was written into.
screen: `A COUSIN READS AT A WEDDING.` → `IT WASN'T WRITTEN FOR WEDDINGS.` → `A CHURCH FALLING APART.`

segments.voice: The writer is Paul, and the church is in Corinth, a busy Greek port city. His first letter to them is full of their problems: rival factions, lawsuits, rich members eating well at the shared meal while poorer ones went hungry. And the Corinthians were proud of their spiritual gifts: speaking in tongues, prophecy, knowledge. So in chapter thirteen Paul says, in effect: without love, all of that is noise. Then he describes love, and the King James Version says it like this: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." Why charity? The Greek word is agape, from the same family of words the Gospels use in the two commandments from a few days ago. Latin translators rendered it caritas, and the King James translators followed with charity, which in their English meant a deep, self-giving love, not only giving money. Newer translations tend to say love. Suffereth long is today's line: love is patient. Read it knowing it was written to people who were quarreling, and it isn't a description of a feeling. It's a list of behaviors, almost a job description. Patient. Kind. Not envious. Not showing off. Not easily provoked. Paul ends the chapter: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Christians read this chapter at weddings and funerals, and some also read it as a picture of how God loves. For a church that was falling apart, the instructions were simple: be patient with each other first.

Christianity, through Paul's hymn: agape, love that is patient and kind, written to a church in pieces. Today's word.

259.title: Christmas, the child
259.hook: Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus, God come as a child in a stable (Luke 2)
259.howItsDone: Christians celebrate Christmas with services on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, many after the four weeks of Advent; many churches set up a nativity scene and read Luke 2 aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Paul's letter to a quarreling church. Your line was love is patient. Today, the last day of our visit to Christianity.

Trees indoors. Lights along the rooflines. A man in a red suit. Songs in the shops from November on. Christmas has collected a lot. Peel it away, layer by layer, and what's underneath is small. A couple far from home, with nowhere proper to stay. A baby, wrapped up tight and laid in an animal's feeding trough. And the first people told about it are shepherds, working the night shift.

segments.voice: Luke chapter two. Mary and Joseph travel to Bethlehem for a census. In the King James words: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." A manger is a feeding trough. Then an angel appears to shepherds in the fields: "Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." Christians call this the incarnation: the belief that God, in Jesus, came into the world not as a king in a palace but as a helpless baby, announced first to laborers. Now the honest part. The Gospels never give a date; December twenty-fifth came later, from the church's calendar, and some Orthodox churches keep Christmas on January seventh because they follow an older calendar. Luke doesn't mention snow, or cold, or a donkey, or any animals at all; the manger is the only hint of them. The word translated inn may simply mean a guest room in a crowded family house. The cold in today's line comes from carols and from how people have pictured it for centuries, not from the text. But the picture has lasted for a reason: a child in the cold is someone you can't ignore. Look back over the week. Two commandments: love your neighbor. The Beatitudes: blessed are the peacemakers. The Lord's Prayer: daily bread. Grace: given, not earned. Easter: new life. Paul: love is patient. And the child, whose birth all of it looks back to.

segments.voice: Picture the scene without the decorations: the trough, the cold night, the shepherds. Then let it move to now: who near you is, in some way, out in the cold? A new neighbor, a lonely relative, someone sleeping outside; hold them a moment, and let one small gift you could give come to you: a coat, a meal, an hour.
